metadata.disclaimer: This resource is for educational purposes. Always verify current law and consult official bar exam materials.
metadata.coverage: MBE subjects + California-specific subjects for California Bar Exam

subjects.name: Torts
subjects.overview: Torts is the area of law dealing with civil wrongs that cause harm or loss, resulting in legal liability for the person who commits the tortious act.

subtopics.name: Battery
subtopics.rule: Battery is the intentional infliction of a harmful or offensive contact with the person of another.
elements: 1. Intent - The defendant acted with purpose or substantial certainty to cause contact
2. Harmful or offensive contact - Contact that causes pain, injury, or would offend a reasonable person's sense of dignity
3. With the person of another - Direct or indirect contact with the plaintiff's body or anything closely connected to it
examples: Punching someone in the face (harmful contact)
Spitting on someone (offensive contact)
Knocking a hat off someone's head (extension of person)
Pulling a chair out from under someone about to sit (indirect contact)
Kissing someone without consent (offensive contact)
defenses: Defense of others (reasonable belief of threat)
subtopics.mnemonics: Battery = Bad Touch (contact required, unlike assault)
subtopics.essayTips: Always check for transferred intent - if D intended to hit A but hit B, battery still applies to B. Discuss whether contact was 'offensive' using reasonable person standard. Don't forget indirect contact (setting a trap, poison).
subtopics.mbeTips: Intent is KEY - look for 'purpose' OR 'substantial certainty.' Defendant need not intend harm, just the contact. Contact with anything closely connected (cane, purse, car plaintiff is in) counts.

subtopics.name: Assault
subtopics.rule: Assault is the intentional creation of a reasonable apprehension in the mind of the victim of an imminent harmful or offensive contact.
elements: 1. Intent - Defendant acted with purpose or substantial certainty to cause apprehension
2. Reasonable apprehension - Plaintiff actually perceived the threat and a reasonable person would have
3. Imminent - The threatened contact must appear to be immediate, not future
4. Harmful or offensive contact - The type of contact threatened must be harmful or offensive
examples: Raising a fist at someone who sees it and fears being struck
Pointing an unloaded gun at plaintiff who believes it's loaded
Swinging a bat at someone's head but missing
Lunging at someone with a knife
notAssault: Threats of future harm ('I'll get you tomorrow')
Contact from behind without prior awareness
subtopics.mnemonics: Assault = Apprehension (fear of contact, no touch needed)
subtopics.essayTips: Contrast with battery - assault requires NO contact but requires awareness. If victim is unaware (sleeping, attacked from behind), no assault. Words alone usually insufficient - need overt act. Apparent ability to carry out threat is sufficient (unloaded gun victim believes is loaded).
subtopics.mbeTips: Watch for 'imminent' - future threats fail. Plaintiff must actually perceive the threat. Apparent ability counts (fake gun). Words + overt act can suffice.

subtopics.name: False Imprisonment
subtopics.rule: False imprisonment is the intentional confinement of another within boundaries fixed by the defendant, without consent or legal privilege.
elements: 1. Intent - Defendant acted with purpose or substantial certainty to confine
2. Confinement - Plaintiff is restricted to a bounded area
3. Awareness or harm - Plaintiff is aware of confinement OR is harmed by it
4. No reasonable means of escape - Plaintiff has no reasonable route of escape known to them
examples: Locking someone in a room
Taking someone's clothes while swimming, leaving them unable to leave
Refusing to stop a moving vehicle when passenger demands to exit
Threatening to harm family member if plaintiff leaves
Invalid use of legal process to confine
notFalseImprisonment: Blocking one exit when another reasonable exit exists
Future threats ('if you leave, I'll fire you tomorrow')

shopkeepersPrivilege.rule: A shopkeeper may detain a suspected shoplifter for a reasonable time, in a reasonable manner, for investigation.
requirements: Reasonable belief of theft
Reasonable duration
Reasonable manner (no excessive force)
Purpose is investigation, not punishment

subtopics.mnemonics: FI = Forced Inside (bounded area, no escape)
subtopics.essayTips: Check if plaintiff knew of a reasonable escape route. The area must be BOUNDED - blocking one direction in an open field is not enough. Note shopkeeper's privilege for retail theft scenarios. Physical force not required - threats and duress count.
subtopics.mbeTips: Confinement can be by physical barriers, threats, duress, or assertion of legal authority. Must be aware OR harmed. Moral pressure alone insufficient. No minimum time required.

subtopics.name: Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress (IIED)
subtopics.rule: IIED occurs when the defendant, by extreme and outrageous conduct, intentionally or recklessly causes severe emotional distress to another.
elements: 1. Extreme and outrageous conduct - Conduct exceeding all bounds of decency tolerated in civilized society
2. Intent or recklessness - Defendant intended to cause distress OR acted with reckless disregard
3. Causation - Defendant's conduct caused the distress
4. Severe emotional distress - Distress beyond what a reasonable person could be expected to endure
outrageousnessFactors: Defendant is in position of authority or power
Defendant knows of plaintiff's particular vulnerability
Defendant is a common carrier or innkeeper
examples: Telling someone falsely that their child has been killed in an accident
Harassing phone calls in the middle of the night repeatedly
Extreme workplace harassment exploiting known vulnerabilities
Debt collector threatening violence against family
Practical joke causing heart attack
notOutrageous: Normal business conduct, even if distressing

bystanderRecovery.rule: A bystander may recover for IIED if present at the scene, closely related to the victim, and defendant knew of their presence.
elements: Plaintiff was present when conduct occurred
Plaintiff was a close family member of the target
Defendant knew or should have known of plaintiff's presence

subtopics.mnemonics: IIED = Intentional Incredibly Evil Deeds (must be EXTREME)
subtopics.essayTips: This is a HIGH bar - emphasize that conduct must be 'beyond all bounds of decency.' Insults alone rarely qualify. Look for vulnerabilities defendant exploited. Physical manifestation of distress helps but is not required in most jurisdictions. Check for bystander recovery if family member witnessed.
subtopics.mbeTips: The conduct must be truly OUTRAGEOUS, not just rude or mean. Consider defendant's knowledge of plaintiff's sensitivity. Recklessness is sufficient for intent. Mere insults = not outrageous.

subtopics.name: Trespass to Land
subtopics.rule: Trespass to land is the intentional physical invasion of another's real property.
elements: 1. Intent - Defendant intended the physical act that resulted in the entry (not intent to trespass)
2. Physical invasion - Defendant or something set in motion by defendant enters the land
3. Another's property - The land belongs to or is in possession of another
examples: Walking onto someone's land without permission
Throwing an object onto someone's property
Flooding a neighbor's land by damming a stream
Shooting bullets or shining lights across property
Remaining on land after permission is revoked
scope: Includes the surface, airspace above, and soil below
Reasonable airspace invasion (normal flight) typically not trespass
subtopics.damages: Nominal damages available without proof of actual harm; actual damages if property damaged.
subtopics.mnemonics: Trespass = 'T'ouching land without permission
subtopics.essayTips: Remember: intent to ENTER, not intent to TRESPASS. Mistake about ownership is not a defense. Includes particles (pollution), water, objects. Continuing trespass = new cause of action each day. Compare with nuisance (interference with USE of land, not physical invasion).
subtopics.mbeTips: Mistake is NOT a defense - if D intends to walk onto land, it's trespass even if D thought it was their land. Physical invasion required (contrast with nuisance). Nominal damages available without actual harm.

subtopics.name: Trespass to Chattels
subtopics.rule: Trespass to chattels is the intentional interference with another's right of possession in personal property, causing some actual harm or deprivation of use.
elements: 1. Intent - Defendant intended the act that interfered with the chattel
2. Interference - Defendant damaged, used, or intermeddled with the property
3. Possession - The property was in another's possession
4. Damages - Actual harm or deprivation of use (unlike trespass to land)
examples: Denting someone's car
Using someone's computer without permission, causing delay
Keeping someone's property for a short time
Damaging someone's animal
subtopics.contrastWithConversion: Trespass to chattels = minor interference; Conversion = major interference warranting forced sale
subtopics.mnemonics: Trespass to Chattels = 'Tampering' with things (minor interference)
subtopics.essayTips: Unlike trespass to land, actual damages required. The key distinction from conversion is severity - if interference is substantial, analyze conversion instead. Consider whether the chattel can be returned in essentially the same condition.
subtopics.mbeTips: Must show ACTUAL damages - unlike trespass to land, no nominal damages for mere touching. Distinguish from conversion based on severity of interference.

subtopics.name: Conversion
subtopics.rule: Conversion is the intentional exercise of dominion or control over another's chattel that so seriously interferes with the owner's rights as to justify requiring the defendant to pay the full value of the property.
elements: 1. Intent - Defendant intended the act of dominion or control
2. Serious interference - The interference substantially deprives the owner of use
3. Over another's chattel - The personal property belongs to another
factorsForSeriousness: Extent of harm to the chattel
Inconvenience and expense to the owner
examples: Stealing someone's car
Selling someone else's property
Substantially damaging or destroying property
Refusing to return property on demand
Materially altering property

remedies.damages: Fair market value at time of conversion (forced sale)

defenses: Good faith purchaser (limited - still liable but in good faith)
subtopics.mnemonics: Conversion = Complete takeover (you bought it now - pay full price)
subtopics.essayTips: This is essentially a 'forced sale' - defendant pays FMV and 'owns' the chattel. Good faith is NOT a defense but may affect damages. Compare severity to trespass to chattels. Analyze whether return is possible and practical.
subtopics.mbeTips: Look at the SEVERITY of interference. Mistake about ownership is NOT a defense. Damages = full FMV. Contrast with trespass to chattels (minor interference, actual damages only).

subtopics.name: Consent
subtopics.rule: Consent is a defense to intentional torts when the plaintiff voluntarily agrees to the defendant's conduct or to the invasion of their interests.

types.rule: Plaintiff explicitly grants permission by words or writing.
limitations: Fraud vitiates consent as to essential nature of act

types.rule: Consent inferred from custom, conduct, or circumstances.
examples: Athletes consent to contact normal to the sport
Emergency medical treatment when patient unconscious
Crowded places - normal jostling

limitations: Cannot consent to criminal acts in most jurisdictions
Consent obtained by fraud (to essential nature) is invalid
Consent obtained by duress is invalid
Exceeding scope of consent removes protection
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish express from implied consent. Analyze whether consent exceeded scope. Check if plaintiff had capacity. Fraud only vitiates if it goes to the essential nature of the act.
subtopics.mbeTips: Consent to being touched ≠ consent to being harmed. Exceeding scope = no defense. Check for incapacity. Emergency implied consent for medical treatment.

subtopics.name: Self-Defense
subtopics.rule: A person may use reasonable force to protect themselves against an imminent threat of harm when they reasonably believe such force is necessary.
elements: 1. Reasonable belief - Defendant reasonably believed they were threatened
2. Imminent threat - Threat must be immediate, not past or future
3. Proportionate response - Force used must be proportionate to threat
4. No excessive force - Cannot use more force than reasonably necessary

deadlyForce.rule: Deadly force is justified only when reasonably necessary to prevent death or serious bodily injury.
restrictions: Must reasonably believe deadly force is about to be used
Majority rule: No duty to retreat before using deadly force
Minority rule: Duty to retreat if safe to do so (except in one's home)

initialAggressor.rule: An initial aggressor generally cannot claim self-defense unless they withdraw and communicate withdrawal.
initialAggressor.exception: If victim responds with excessive force, initial aggressor may defend against that excess

subtopics.mnemonics: Self-defense = Reasonable Response to Real threat (3 Rs)
subtopics.essayTips: Always analyze proportionality - deadly force only for deadly threats. Check if defendant was initial aggressor. Discuss retreat rules if applicable. Reasonable BELIEF standard - mistaken belief may still be protected if reasonable.
subtopics.mbeTips: Objective reasonableness standard. No duty to retreat in majority. Initial aggressor loses defense unless withdrawal. Can only meet force with like force.

subtopics.name: Defense of Others
subtopics.rule: A person may use reasonable force to defend another person when they reasonably believe that person is being threatened with imminent harm.
elements: 1. Reasonable belief - Defendant reasonably believed third party was threatened
2. Proportionate force - Force used must match the perceived threat
3. Privilege extends as far as the third party's own right to defend
subtopics.modernRule: Majority rule: Defendant judged by reasonable appearances, even if mistaken about actual threat (reasonable mistake permitted).
subtopics.oldRule: Minority/Old rule: Defendant 'stands in the shoes' of the person defended - if that person had no privilege, neither does defendant.
subtopics.mnemonics: Defense of Others = You can be someone's hero (reasonable belief standard)
subtopics.essayTips: Most jurisdictions now use reasonable appearances test. Analyze what a reasonable person would believe. Force must be proportionate to apparent threat.
subtopics.mbeTips: Modern rule: Reasonable belief test. Mistake is allowed if reasonable. Cannot use more force than the threatened person could use.

subtopics.name: Defense of Property
subtopics.rule: A person may use reasonable non-deadly force to protect their real or personal property from invasion or theft.
elements: 1. Reasonable belief - Defendant reasonably believed property was threatened
2. Non-deadly force only - Deadly force NEVER permitted merely to defend property
3. Request to desist - Generally must first request intruder to leave (if practical)

realProperty.rule: Owner may use reasonable force to prevent or terminate unlawful entry.
limitations: Must first request departure if practical
Spring guns/traps generally not permitted (deadly force)

personalProperty.rule: Owner may use reasonable force to prevent theft or recover chattel.

recaptureOfChattels.rule: Owner may use reasonable force to recapture chattels if in 'fresh pursuit'.
requirements: Wrongful taking (not voluntary transfer)
Fresh pursuit (without unreasonable delay)
Reasonable force only

subtopics.mnemonics: Defense of Property = No Death for Stuff (deadly force prohibited)
subtopics.essayTips: CRITICAL: No deadly force to protect property. Spring gun/trap cases = classic bar exam issue. Fresh pursuit required for recapture of chattels. Analyze whether request to leave was practical.
subtopics.mbeTips: Never deadly force for property alone. Spring guns = not allowed. Fresh pursuit needed for recapture. Force must be reasonable and proportionate.

subtopics.name: Necessity
subtopics.rule: A person may interfere with the property of another to prevent greater harm, if the interference is reasonable and necessary.

types.rule: Complete defense when acting to protect the public from a significant threat.
types.example: Firefighters destroying home to create firebreak protecting town

types.rule: Qualified defense when acting to protect oneself or one's own property.
types.damages: Must pay for actual damages caused
types.example: Mooring boat to someone's dock during sudden storm
rights: May enter and remain as long as necessity exists
Owner cannot expel during continuing necessity
Must compensate for actual harm caused

limitations: Response must be proportionate to threat
subtopics.mnemonics: Public = Free pass, Private = Pay for damages
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish public (complete defense) from private (pay for damages). Ploof v. Putnam is the classic private necessity case. Vincent v. Lake Erie - must still pay for damages. Owner cannot eject during continuing necessity.
subtopics.mbeTips: Public necessity = complete defense, no payment. Private necessity = privilege to enter but must pay damages. Cannot be expelled during ongoing emergency.

subtopics.name: Negligence - Overview
subtopics.rule: Negligence is conduct that falls below the standard of care established by law for the protection of others against unreasonable risk of harm.
elements: 1. Duty - Defendant owed a duty of care to plaintiff
2. Breach - Defendant breached that duty
3. Causation - Defendant's breach caused plaintiff's harm (actual and proximate)
4. Damages - Plaintiff suffered actual harm
subtopics.mnemonics: DBCD = Duty, Breach, Causation, Damages
subtopics.essayTips: Always analyze all four elements systematically. Many essays turn on duty or proximate cause issues. Don't forget to consider defenses after establishing prima facie case.
subtopics.mbeTips: Process of elimination - if any element is missing, no negligence. Duty questions often involve scope of duty. Causation is frequently tested.

subtopics.name: Duty of Care
subtopics.rule: The general duty is to act as a reasonable person would under the same or similar circumstances.

generalDuty.rule: All persons owe a duty to all foreseeable plaintiffs to exercise reasonable care.
generalDuty.foreseeablePlaintiff: Palsgraf rule - duty is owed only to those within the foreseeable zone of danger

standardsOfCare.rule: Objective standard - what would a reasonable person of ordinary prudence do
factors: Mental characteristics NOT considered (low intelligence, inexperience)
Knowledge possessed by defendant is considered

standardsOfCare.rule: Held to standard of a reasonably competent member of that profession
specialRules: Specialists held to higher standard within specialty
Doctors: Historically locality rule, now generally national standard
Informed consent: Must disclose material risks

standardsOfCare.rule: Child of similar age, intelligence, and experience
standardsOfCare.exception: Adult standard applies when child engages in adult activities (driving, operating powerboats)

subtopics.mnemonics: Reasonable Person = 'What Would a Normal Adult Do?' (WWNAD)
subtopics.essayTips: Identify who the plaintiff is and whether they are foreseeable. Apply correct standard based on defendant's status. For professionals, discuss applicable standard of care within the profession.
subtopics.mbeTips: Physical disabilities considered, mental disabilities NOT. Child standard unless adult activity. Professionals judged by their profession's standards.

subtopics.name: Special Duty Rules
Duty to Rescue/Affirmative Acts
subtopics.rule: Generally, there is no duty to rescue or assist a stranger in peril.
exceptions: Defendant undertook to rescue (must continue with reasonable care)
Statutory duty (Good Samaritan laws may impose or protect)

subtopics.name: Landowner Duties

traditionalRules.duty: Only refrain from willful/wanton conduct; no concealed traps
traditionalRules.discoveredTrespasser: Once discovered, duty to warn of known dangers

traditionalRules.duty: Warn of known concealed dangers; no duty to inspect
Reasonable care to inspect and discover dangers and make safe or warn

subtopics.modernTrend: Many jurisdictions abandon categories; apply reasonable care to all entrants

attractiveNuisance.rule: Landowner owes duty of care to trespassing children for artificial conditions if:
elements: 1. Owner knows or should know children likely to trespass
2. Condition poses unreasonable risk of serious injury/death to children
3. Children don't appreciate the danger due to their youth
4. Utility of condition is slight compared to risk
5. Owner fails to use reasonable care to protect children

subtopics.name: Negligent Infliction of Emotional Distress (NIED)
subtopics.rule: Plaintiff may recover for emotional distress negligently caused by defendant.

approaches.rule: Plaintiff must be within zone of physical danger from defendant's negligence
approaches.requirements: Physical impact or threat of impact required

approaches.rule: Bystander may recover for witnessing injury to close family member
factors: Present at scene and witnessed the injury

subtopics.physicalManifestation: Some jurisdictions require physical symptoms of distress

subtopics.essayTips: Landowner duty questions: First identify status of entrant. Note trend toward single standard. Attractive nuisance is frequently tested. NIED: Know whether jurisdiction follows zone of danger or bystander approach.
subtopics.mbeTips: Know the three categories of entrants and duties owed. Attractive nuisance is for ARTIFICIAL conditions only. Bystander NIED requires presence at scene and close family relationship.

subtopics.name: Breach of Duty
subtopics.rule: Breach occurs when defendant's conduct falls below the applicable standard of care.

tests.name: Hand Formula (Risk-Utility)
tests.rule: Breach if B < P x L (burden of precaution less than probability times magnitude of harm)

tests.name: Custom
tests.rule: Industry custom is relevant but not conclusive evidence of reasonable care

tests.name: Violation of Statute (Negligence Per Se)
tests.rule: Violation of a safety statute may establish breach if:
elements: 1. Plaintiff is within the class of persons the statute protects
2. Harm is of the type the statute was designed to prevent
tests.effect: Violation is conclusive on breach unless excuse applies

tests.name: Res Ipsa Loquitur
tests.rule: The thing speaks for itself - inference of negligence from the nature of the accident
elements: 1. The accident is of a kind that ordinarily does not occur without negligence
2. The instrumentality was in defendant's exclusive control
3. Plaintiff did not contribute to the accident
tests.effect: Creates inference of negligence; may permit case to go to jury

subtopics.mnemonics: Negligence Per Se = 'Plaintiff in Protected class, Harm of intended type'
subtopics.essayTips: Analyze breach using reasonable person standard, then check for negligence per se or res ipsa. Custom is evidence but not dispositive (TJ Hooper). Res ipsa is an evidentiary tool when specific acts unknown.
subtopics.mbeTips: Negligence per se requires both protected class AND type of harm. Res ipsa requires exclusive control. Compliance with statute is evidence of due care but not conclusive.

subtopics.name: Actual Causation (Cause in Fact)
subtopics.rule: Defendant's conduct must be the actual cause of plaintiff's harm.

tests.name: But-For Test
tests.rule: But for defendant's negligent conduct, would plaintiff's injury have occurred?

tests.name: Substantial Factor Test
tests.rule: Used when multiple causes each sufficient to cause harm
tests.application: Each defendant's conduct must be a substantial factor in causing harm
tests.example: Two fires merge and burn plaintiff's property - both tortfeasors liable

tests.name: Alternative Causation (Summers v. Tice)
tests.rule: When two defendants act negligently but only one caused harm, burden shifts to each to prove they did not cause injury
requirements: All possible tortfeasors before the court
Each acted negligently
Plaintiff cannot identify which caused harm

tests.name: Market Share Liability
tests.rule: In DES-type cases, manufacturers liable in proportion to market share
requirements: Fungible product
Plaintiff unable to identify specific manufacturer
Substantial share of market before court

lostChance.rule: Some jurisdictions allow recovery for negligently reduced chance of survival

subtopics.mnemonics: But-For = 'Would it have happened anyway?'
subtopics.essayTips: But-for test works in most cases. Switch to substantial factor for concurrent sufficient causes. Summers v. Tice for alternative liability (both shot, one hit). Market share for fungible products.
subtopics.mbeTips: But-for is default. Substantial factor when multiple sufficient causes. Burden shifting in alternative liability. Market share is rare but testable.

subtopics.name: Proximate Causation (Legal Cause)
subtopics.rule: Defendant is liable only for harms that are within the scope of the foreseeable risk created by defendant's negligence.

tests.name: Foreseeability Test
tests.rule: Was the type of harm foreseeable as a result of defendant's conduct?
tests.palsgraf: Defendant liable only for harms to foreseeable plaintiffs from foreseeable risks

tests.name: Direct Cause Test
tests.rule: Defendant liable for all direct consequences, however unforeseeable (minority view)

interveningCauses.rule: An intervening cause breaks the chain of causation only if it is a superseding cause.
notSuperseding: Medical malpractice in treating plaintiff's injury
Subsequent accident caused by original injury

eggshellPlaintiff.rule: Defendant takes plaintiff as they find them - liable for full extent of injuries even if unforeseeable due to plaintiff's preexisting condition
eggshellPlaintiff.note: TYPE of harm must be foreseeable, but EXTENT need not be

subtopics.mnemonics: Proximate Cause = 'Foreseeable harm to foreseeable plaintiff'
subtopics.essayTips: Foreseeability is key - was the TYPE of harm within the risk? Eggshell plaintiff means extent doesn't matter. Analyze whether intervening acts are superseding. Criminal acts usually supersede but not if foreseeable.
subtopics.mbeTips: Focus on foreseeability of TYPE of harm. Eggshell plaintiff = no limit on damages for preexisting conditions. Medical malpractice is foreseeable and does not supersede. Rescuers are foreseeable.

subtopics.name: Damages
subtopics.rule: Plaintiff must prove actual damages to recover in negligence.

categories: Economic: Medical expenses, lost wages, property damage
Non-economic: Pain and suffering, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment

types.rule: NOT available in negligence - actual harm required
Available only for reckless or willful conduct, not ordinary negligence

collateralSource.rule: Benefits received from independent sources (insurance) do not reduce defendant's liability

mitigationDuty.rule: Plaintiff must take reasonable steps to mitigate damages after injury

wrongfulDeath.rule: Statutory action for death caused by defendant's tortious conduct

survivalAction.rule: Decedent's own claims survive death and may be brought by estate
survivalAction.damages: What decedent could have recovered if they had lived

subtopics.mnemonics: Negligence Needs ACTUAL harm (no nominal damages)
subtopics.essayTips: Always prove actual damages - no nominal damages in negligence. Collateral source rule means don't reduce for insurance. Discuss mitigation duty. Distinguish wrongful death from survival actions.
subtopics.mbeTips: Actual damages required. Collateral source = no reduction for insurance. Mitigation duty exists. Know difference between wrongful death and survival actions.

subtopics.name: Contributory Negligence
subtopics.rule: Traditional rule: Plaintiff's own negligence, however slight, completely bars recovery.
subtopics.jurisdictions: Only followed in Alabama, Maryland, North Carolina, Virginia, DC

lastClearChance.rule: Doctrine that allows plaintiff to recover despite contributory negligence if defendant had the last clear chance to avoid the harm
lastClearChance.helpless: Defendant discovered or should have discovered plaintiff's peril

subtopics.mnemonics: Contributory = Complete bar (harsh old rule)
subtopics.essayTips: Identify which negligence regime applies. If contributory, always discuss last clear chance. Compare to modern comparative negligence.
subtopics.mbeTips: Most jurisdictions have abandoned contributory negligence. Know last clear chance doctrine. Watch for jurisdiction-specific questions.

subtopics.name: Comparative Negligence
subtopics.rule: Modern rule: Plaintiff's damages reduced in proportion to their own fault.

types.rule: Plaintiff recovers their percentage of damages regardless of fault percentage
types.example: Plaintiff 90% at fault can still recover 10% of damages

types.rule: Plaintiff barred from recovery if 50% or more at fault
types.example: Plaintiff 49% at fault recovers 51% of damages; 50% recovers nothing

types.rule: Plaintiff barred from recovery if 51% or more at fault
types.example: Plaintiff 50% at fault recovers 50%; 51% recovers nothing

subtopics.mnemonics: Comparative = Cut by percentage
subtopics.essayTips: Always identify which type of comparative negligence applies. Calculate percentages. Most bar exams use pure comparative unless otherwise stated. Note that many intentional torts do not reduce for comparative fault.
subtopics.mbeTips: Pure = always recover something. Modified = bars at 50% or 51%. Calculate recovery carefully. Check if jurisdiction is pure or modified.

subtopics.name: Assumption of Risk
subtopics.rule: Plaintiff who voluntarily assumes a known risk may be barred from or limited in recovery.

types.rule: Written waiver/release of liability
types.validity: Generally enforceable except for essential services, gross negligence, intentional acts, or public policy violations

types.rule: Plaintiff impliedly consents to risks inherent in an activity
types.example: Baseball spectator hit by foul ball

types.rule: Plaintiff knowingly encounters a risk created by defendant's negligence
types.effect: In comparative negligence jurisdictions, merges into comparative fault analysis

elements: 1. Knowledge of the risk
2. Appreciation of the risk
3. Voluntary encounter with the risk
subtopics.mnemonics: Assumption = 'A-Knew and A-Chose to Encounter'
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish primary (no duty, complete bar) from secondary (comparative fault analysis). Express waivers: Check for essential services, gross negligence, unequal bargaining power. Sports/recreation cases often involve primary assumption.
subtopics.mbeTips: Know the types and effects. Express waivers valid in most contexts but not essential services. Primary = complete bar. Secondary = merged with comparative fault in most jurisdictions.

subtopics.name: Strict Liability - Overview
subtopics.rule: Defendant is liable regardless of fault for harm caused by certain activities or things.
categories: Domestic animals with known dangerous propensities

subtopics.name: Abnormally Dangerous Activities
subtopics.rule: One who carries on an abnormally dangerous activity is strictly liable for resulting harm.
factors: 1. High degree of risk of harm
2. Likelihood that harm will be great
3. Inability to eliminate risk by reasonable care
4. Extent to which activity is not common
6. Extent to which value to community is outweighed by danger
examples: Blasting/explosives
Storage of large quantities of explosives or flammables
Crop dusting
Fumigation with toxic gases
Keeping wild animals

scope.rule: Strict liability applies only to harm within the type of risk that makes the activity abnormally dangerous
scope.example: Blasting - liable for harm from explosion/vibration, not for truck running over pedestrian while transporting explosives

subtopics.mnemonics: Abnormally Dangerous = Can't make it safe no matter how careful
subtopics.essayTips: Apply the six-factor test. Focus on inability to eliminate risk with care. Scope limitation is important - only liable for risks that make activity dangerous. Compare with negligence for activities that don't qualify.
subtopics.mbeTips: Key factor: Cannot be made safe with reasonable care. Common activities rarely qualify. Harm must be from the type of risk that makes it dangerous.

subtopics.name: Animals

rules.rule: Strict liability for injuries caused by wild animals kept by defendant
rules.scope: Harm must be from dangerous propensity characteristic of the species

rules.rule: Strict liability only if owner knew or should have known of animal's dangerous propensity
rules.onebitere: Once an animal has shown dangerous tendencies, owner is strictly liable for future incidents

rules.rule: Owner strictly liable for foreseeable damage by livestock/animals trespassing on another's land
rules.exceptions: Cats and dogs (negligence only); animals on public road

subtopics.mnemonics: Wild = Always strict; Domestic = 'One bite' rule (known propensity needed)
subtopics.essayTips: Classify the animal first - wild or domestic. For domestic animals, analyze knowledge of propensity. Trespassing livestock is separate doctrine. Scope limitation applies to wild animals.
subtopics.mbeTips: Wild animals = automatic strict liability. Domestic = need prior knowledge. 'One bite' is a misnomer - any known propensity counts, not just biting.

subtopics.name: Products Liability - Overview
subtopics.rule: Manufacturers, distributors, and sellers may be liable for injuries caused by defective products.
subtopics.mnemonics: Products Liability = Three theories: Negligence, Strict Liability, Warranty
subtopics.essayTips: Analyze all three theories when applicable. Check who is in the chain of distribution. Consider whether defendant is a commercial seller. Note statute of limitations and repose issues.
subtopics.mbeTips: Know all three theories. Commercial sellers only for strict liability. Negligence available against any defendant. Warranty depends on privity rules.

subtopics.name: Strict Products Liability
subtopics.rule: A commercial seller who sells a defective product that is unreasonably dangerous is strictly liable for harm caused to users or consumers.
elements: 1. Commercial seller or distributor
2. Defective product
3. Defect existed when product left defendant's control
4. Defect caused plaintiff's harm
5. Plaintiff is a foreseeable user or bystander

defectTypes.rule: Product departs from its intended design
defectTypes.test: Does this unit differ from other products from the same line?
defectTypes.example: Car with improperly installed brake line

defectTypes.rule: All products of that design are defective

tests.name: Consumer Expectations Test
tests.rule: Product fails to meet safety expectations of an ordinary consumer

tests.name: Risk-Utility Test
tests.rule: Risk of harm outweighs benefits of design; reasonable alternative design available

defectTypes.example: SUV prone to rollover due to high center of gravity

defectTypes.rule: Inadequate warnings or instructions render product defective
defectTypes.duty: Must warn of foreseeable risks of harm
defectTypes.learnedIntermediary: For prescription drugs, warning to physician may satisfy duty
defectTypes.example: Medication without warning of dangerous side effects

subtopics.mnemonics: Three Defects: Make, Design, Warn (MDW)
subtopics.essayTips: Identify the defect type first. Manufacturing = deviation from design. Design = all products have the defect. Warnings = analyze what was disclosed and what should have been. Learned intermediary doctrine for prescription drugs.
subtopics.mbeTips: Distinguish the three defect types. Risk-utility test is most common for design defects. Manufacturer has duty to warn of foreseeable misuse. Bystanders can recover.

subtopics.name: Products Liability Defenses

defenses.rule: In comparative fault jurisdictions, plaintiff's negligence reduces recovery
defenses.application: Applies to misuse, failure to follow instructions, or failure to discover defect

defenses.rule: Plaintiff who knowingly and voluntarily uses defective product may be barred
defenses.requirements: Actual knowledge of specific defect and its danger

defenses.rule: Unforeseeable misuse may bar or reduce recovery
defenses.note: Foreseeable misuse does NOT bar recovery - manufacturer must anticipate

defenses.rule: Substantial unforeseeable alteration after sale may bar recovery
defenses.note: Modification that does not cause the injury is not a defense

defenses.rule: Compliance with government standards is evidence of non-defect but not conclusive
Evidence that safer design was not feasible - relevant to risk-utility analysis

notDefenses: Disclaimer or waiver (generally unenforceable for personal injury)
Lack of privity (not required for strict liability or negligence)
Contributory negligence (minority view - generally merged with comparative fault)
subtopics.essayTips: Analyze whether misuse or alteration was foreseeable. Comparative fault applies in most jurisdictions. Waivers ineffective for personal injury in strict products liability.
subtopics.mbeTips: Foreseeable misuse is not a defense - must be unforeseeable. Privity is NOT required for strict liability or negligence. Disclaimers don't work for personal injury claims.

subtopics.name: Respondeat Superior
subtopics.rule: An employer is vicariously liable for the tortious acts of employees committed within the scope of employment.
elements: 1. Employer-employee relationship (not independent contractor)
2. Tortious act by employee
3. Act within scope of employment

within: Acts of the kind hired to perform
Acts occurring substantially within authorized time and place
Acts motivated, at least in part, by purpose of serving employer
outside: Frolic: Substantial departure from employment duties
Intentional torts (unless foreseeable or in furtherance of employment)
scopeOfEmployment.detour: Minor deviation from employment - still within scope

comingAndGoing.rule: Commuting to/from work generally not within scope
exceptions: Travel is integral part of job

subtopics.mnemonics: Scope = 'Serving the boss's purposes, not frolic'
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish frolic (major departure, no liability) from detour (minor, liability). Analyze whether employee was serving employer's interests. Intentional torts require special analysis. Coming and going rule is frequently tested.
subtopics.mbeTips: Frolic = outside scope. Detour = within scope. Coming and going generally excludes commuting. Intentional torts may be within scope if job-related.

subtopics.name: Independent Contractors
subtopics.rule: Generally, a principal is NOT vicariously liable for the torts of an independent contractor.
exceptions: Non-delegable duties (inherently dangerous activities, duty to maintain property)
Apparent authority (contractor appears to be employee)
Employer retains control over the work

factors: Control over manner and means of work (key factor)
Whether work is regular business of employer

subtopics.mnemonics: IC = 'I Control my own work' (no vicarious liability)
subtopics.essayTips: First determine if relationship is employee or IC. If IC, analyze exceptions. Control is the key factor. Non-delegable duties are frequently tested (inherently dangerous activities).
subtopics.mbeTips: Control is the key factor for employee vs IC. Know the exceptions to IC non-liability. Non-delegable duties cannot be delegated to ICs.

subtopics.name: Joint and Several Liability
subtopics.rule: Each tortfeasor is independently liable for the entire amount of plaintiff's damages.

contribution.rule: Joint tortfeasor who pays more than their share may seek contribution from others
methods: Comparative fault shares (by percentage of fault)

indemnity.rule: Complete shifting of loss from one tortfeasor to another
situations: Vicarious liability (employer seeks indemnity from employee)
Strict liability retailer seeks indemnity from manufacturer

subtopics.modernTrend: Many jurisdictions have modified joint and several liability to proportional liability or hybrid approaches
subtopics.mnemonics: Joint & Several = 'Sue one for all, then they sort it out'
subtopics.essayTips: Discuss whether joint and several applies or if jurisdiction uses several liability only. Analyze contribution rights among defendants. Indemnity is appropriate in vicarious liability and products liability chain cases.
subtopics.mbeTips: Many jurisdictions have modified joint and several. Know contribution (sharing) vs indemnity (complete shift). Comparative fault has affected these rules significantly.

subtopics.name: Private Nuisance
subtopics.rule: A private nuisance is a substantial and unreasonable interference with another's use and enjoyment of their land.
elements: 1. Substantial interference - More than slight inconvenience; offensive to normal person
2. Unreasonable interference - Gravity of harm outweighs utility of conduct
3. Use and enjoyment - Affects plaintiff's ability to use their property
factors: Ability of plaintiff to avoid harm
Ability of defendant to prevent harm
subtopics.mnemonics: Private Nuisance = Neighbor's nasty conduct affecting YOUR property enjoyment
subtopics.essayTips: Balance gravity of harm vs. utility of conduct. Coming to the nuisance is not a complete bar but is a factor. Distinguish from trespass (physical invasion vs. interference with use). Hypersensitive plaintiffs don't set the standard.
subtopics.mbeTips: Requires interference with USE, not physical invasion. Balancing test - gravity vs. utility. Coming to nuisance is NOT a bar. Abnormally sensitive plaintiffs don't recover for that sensitivity.

subtopics.name: Public Nuisance
subtopics.rule: A public nuisance is an unreasonable interference with a right common to the general public.
examples: Obstruction of public roads
Pollution of navigable waters
Operating illegal gambling establishment
Maintaining conditions conducive to disease

whoCanSue.publicAuthorities: Government officials can seek abatement or damages
whoCanSue.privateParties: Only if suffering special damage different in kind from general public

specialDamage.rule: Private plaintiff must show harm different in KIND (not just degree) from that suffered by public
specialDamage.example: Obstruction of highway: General delay (no standing) vs. blocked access to plaintiff's property (special damage)

subtopics.mnemonics: Public Nuisance = Harm to community; private suit needs SPECIAL damage
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish from private nuisance. For private suit, emphasize special damage requirement - different in KIND from public. Public authorities can always sue.
subtopics.mbeTips: Private plaintiff needs special damage different in kind, not just degree. Public officials can always sue for public nuisances.

subtopics.name: Defamation - Elements
subtopics.rule: Defamation is the publication of a false statement of fact that causes injury to another's reputation.
elements: 1. Defamatory statement - Statement that tends to harm reputation, expose to hatred/contempt, or discourage others from associating
2. Of and concerning the plaintiff - Statement is reasonably understood to refer to plaintiff
3. Publication - Communication to at least one third party
4. Falsity - Statement is false (constitutional requirement)
5. Fault - At least negligence, or actual malice for public figures
6. Damages - Harm to reputation (or presumed in some cases)

types.rule: Written or permanently recorded defamation
types.damages: Presumed in many jurisdictions (libel per se)

types.rule: Spoken defamation
types.damages: Must prove special damages unless slander per se

categories: Conduct incompatible with business or profession
slanderPerSe.effect: Damages presumed; no proof of special damages required

subtopics.mnemonics: DPPFD = Defamatory, Publication, Plaintiff identified, Falsity, Damages. Slander per se = 'Business, Loathsome, Criminal, Unchaste' (BLCU)
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish libel from slander. For slander, check if per se category applies. Analyze fault standard based on plaintiff's status. Note opinion is protected. Publication to one person is enough.
subtopics.mbeTips: Know slander per se categories - damages presumed. Libel per se often presumed too. One third party is sufficient publication. Each republication is new defamation.

subtopics.name: Constitutional Defamation Standards
subtopics.rule: The First Amendment imposes fault requirements beyond common law.

plaintiffCategories.definition: Government employees with substantial responsibility for government affairs
plaintiffCategories.standard: Actual malice required (New York Times v. Sullivan)
plaintiffCategories.scope: Official conduct or fitness for office

subtypes.name: Limited-Purpose Public Figure
subtypes.definition: Voluntarily injected themselves into particular public controversy
subtypes.standard: Actual malice for statements related to that controversy

plaintiffCategories.standard: At least negligence required (Gertz v. Welch)
plaintiffCategories.stateOption: States may allow presumed/punitive damages only with actual malice

actualMalice.definition: Knowledge of falsity OR reckless disregard for truth or falsity

subtopics.mnemonics: Actual Malice = Knew it was false or didn't care if it was false
subtopics.essayTips: Classify plaintiff FIRST - this determines fault standard. Actual malice is a constitutional standard, not common law malice. Private figures get more protection. Analyze whether public controversy exists for limited-purpose public figures.
subtopics.mbeTips: Public official/figure = actual malice. Private figure = negligence (minimum). Actual malice = knowledge of falsity OR reckless disregard. NOT mere negligence or failure to investigate.

subtopics.name: Defamation Defenses and Privileges

defenses.rule: Complete defense - truth is an absolute bar to defamation liability
Pure opinion is protected, but opinion implying false facts may be actionable
defenses.test: Would a reasonable listener understand as asserting facts?

types: Judicial proceedings (statements by parties, witnesses, lawyers, judges)
Fair report privilege (accurate reports of official proceedings)
Common interest privilege (statements to those sharing legitimate interest)

subtopics.mnemonics: Absolute = Cannot be lost; Qualified = Can be abused away
subtopics.essayTips: Always check for truth first. Distinguish absolute from qualified privileges. Qualified privileges can be lost by abuse. Fair report privilege requires accuracy about the proceeding.
subtopics.mbeTips: Truth is absolute defense. Opinion is protected but fact-implying opinions are not. Qualified privileges can be lost by abuse or excessive publication.

subtopics.name: Intrusion Upon Seclusion
subtopics.rule: Intentional intrusion upon the solitude or seclusion of another that would be highly offensive to a reasonable person.
elements: 1. Intentional intrusion - Deliberate act of prying
2. Into private affairs - Area in which plaintiff has reasonable expectation of privacy
3. Highly offensive - Would offend a reasonable person's sense of privacy
examples: Wiretapping phone calls
Secret recording in private spaces
Peeping into windows
Reading private mail or email
Persistent surveillance
subtopics.note: No publication required - the intrusion itself is the tort
subtopics.mnemonics: Intrusion = 'I'm invading your space' (no publication needed)
subtopics.essayTips: No publication required - distinguish from disclosure. Analyze reasonable expectation of privacy. Highly offensive standard is objective. Public places generally not protected.
subtopics.mbeTips: NO publication required. Requires reasonable expectation of privacy. Public places = no expectation. Focus on the intrusion itself.

subtopics.name: Public Disclosure of Private Facts
subtopics.rule: Publicizing private information about another that would be highly offensive to a reasonable person and is not of legitimate public concern.
elements: 1. Public disclosure - Widespread communication to the public
2. Private facts - True information not publicly known
3. Highly offensive - Would offend a reasonable person
4. Not newsworthy - Not of legitimate public concern
notActionable: Disclosure to one person or small group
subtopics.mnemonics: Disclosure = 'Don't tell everyone my true secrets'
subtopics.essayTips: Must be WIDESPREAD disclosure, not just to one person. Truth is NOT a defense (unlike defamation). Newsworthiness is a complete defense. Distinguish from defamation - this involves TRUE facts.
subtopics.mbeTips: Truth is NOT a defense. Requires widespread publication. Newsworthy = not actionable. Public records are fair game.

subtopics.name: False Light
subtopics.rule: Publicizing information that places another in a false light that would be highly offensive to a reasonable person.
elements: 1. Publication - Widespread communication
2. False light - Creates false impression about plaintiff
3. Highly offensive - Would offend a reasonable person
4. Fault - Actual malice for matters of public concern
examples: Using plaintiff's photo next to unrelated scandalous story
Attributing views to plaintiff they don't hold
Fictional accounts presented as true
contrastWithDefamation: False light need not damage reputation
Different focus: defamation = reputation; false light = mental distress
subtopics.mnemonics: False Light = 'You made me look bad/weird with false impression'
subtopics.essayTips: Overlaps significantly with defamation but focus is different. Doesn't require damage to reputation. May cover non-defamatory falsehoods. Some states don't recognize this tort.
subtopics.mbeTips: Widespread publication required (unlike defamation). Focus is on false impression, not reputation. Some jurisdictions don't recognize it.

subtopics.name: Appropriation of Name or Likeness
subtopics.rule: Using another's name, likeness, or identity for commercial advantage without consent.
elements: 1. Appropriation - Use of name, likeness, or identity
2. For commercial purpose - Usually advertising or trade
3. Without consent - No permission granted
examples: Using celebrity photo in advertisement without permission
Using someone's name to endorse product
Using look-alike or sound-alike to evoke celebrity

rightOfPublicity.rule: Related but distinct - protects commercial value of celebrity identity
differences: Focuses on economic interest, not privacy

subtopics.mnemonics: Appropriation = 'You're using ME to make money'
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish from right of publicity. Commercial purpose is key. Newsworthiness is a defense. Celebrity look-alikes/sound-alikes may be covered.
subtopics.mbeTips: Must be commercial use. News/editorial use is protected. Right of publicity is related but distinct. Consent is complete defense.

subtopics.name: Intentional Misrepresentation (Fraud/Deceit)
subtopics.rule: A false representation of material fact, made with knowledge of falsity and intent to induce reliance, upon which plaintiff justifiably relies to their detriment.
elements: 1. False representation - Of existing material fact (not opinion or future intent)
2. Scienter - Knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for truth
3. Intent to induce reliance - Purpose of inducing plaintiff to act
4. Justifiable reliance - Plaintiff actually and reasonably relied
5. Damages - Economic loss caused by reliance
whatCounts: Nondisclosure when duty to speak exists
dutyToDisclose: Known reliance on defendant's specialized knowledge
subtopics.mnemonics: Fraud = FRIDR (False statement, Reliance, Intent, Damages, Reasonable reliance)
subtopics.essayTips: Analyze each element carefully. Scienter is key - knowledge or recklessness. Opinion generally not actionable unless speaker has superior knowledge. Check for duty to disclose if no affirmative statement.
subtopics.mbeTips: Must be statement of FACT, not opinion (generally). Scienter = knowledge or recklessness. Puffery not actionable. Damages = pecuniary loss.

subtopics.name: Negligent Misrepresentation
subtopics.rule: A false statement made without reasonable care as to its truth, in a business or professional context, to guide others in business transactions.
elements: 1. False statement - Regarding material fact
2. Breach of duty of care - In obtaining or communicating information
3. Business or professional context - Information provided in commercial setting
4. Intent for guidance - Statement meant to guide business transactions
5. Justifiable reliance - By plaintiff or known limited group
6. Damages - Pecuniary loss

limitedLiability.rule: Liability limited to those for whose guidance information was supplied or known limited group

subtopics.mnemonics: Negligent Misrepresentation = Careless commercial statements
subtopics.essayTips: Narrower scope than fraud - only liable to known group. Must be business/professional context. Compare with fraud elements. Pecuniary loss required.
subtopics.mbeTips: Limited to known group or class. Business/professional context required. Negligence, not scienter. Pecuniary damages only.

subtopics.name: Malicious Prosecution
subtopics.rule: Wrongfully initiating criminal proceedings against another.
elements: 1. Institution of criminal proceedings - Defendant initiated prosecution
2. Without probable cause - No reasonable basis to believe plaintiff guilty
3. With malice - Improper purpose beyond bringing offender to justice
4. Termination in plaintiff's favor - Proceedings ended favorably to plaintiff
5. Damages - Injury to plaintiff
favorableTermination: Nolle prosequi (not abandonment for practical reasons)
subtopics.mnemonics: Malicious Prosecution = Criminal case + No probable cause + Malice + Win
subtopics.essayTips: Requires favorable termination FIRST. Analyze whether there was probable cause. Malice can be inferred from lack of probable cause. Heavy burden - disfavored action.
subtopics.mbeTips: Must terminate in plaintiff's favor first. Probable cause negates claim. Malice = improper purpose. High burden of proof.

subtopics.name: Abuse of Process
subtopics.rule: Using civil or criminal process for an improper collateral purpose.
elements: 1. Legal process - Legitimate process was used
2. Improper purpose - Process used for purpose for which it was not designed
3. Act or threat - Perverting the process in some way
subtopics.distinction: Unlike malicious prosecution, process may have been properly issued; the MISUSE is the wrong
examples: Using subpoena power to harass
Filing suit solely to coerce unrelated settlement
Using attachment to extort
subtopics.mnemonics: Abuse of Process = 'Right process, wrong purpose'
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish from malicious prosecution - no need for favorable termination. Focus is on misuse of proper process. Must identify the improper collateral purpose.
subtopics.mbeTips: No favorable termination required. Process was proper but misused. Look for collateral/ulterior purpose.

keyDistinctions.explanation: Battery requires harmful or offensive CONTACT; Assault requires APPREHENSION of imminent contact, no contact needed. Battery victim need not be aware; Assault victim must perceive the threat.
Trespass requires physical invasion; Nuisance requires interference with use and enjoyment (can be noise, odors, etc. without physical invasion).
Trespass to chattels = minor interference, actual damages required, property can be returned. Conversion = serious interference, forced sale remedy, defendant pays FMV.
Intentional torts require intent (purpose or substantial certainty). Negligence requires only failure to exercise reasonable care. Different defenses apply.
Contributory negligence completely bars recovery (minority rule). Comparative negligence reduces recovery proportionally (majority rule).
Negligence requires showing defendant failed to exercise reasonable care. Strict liability imposes liability regardless of care exercised (abnormally dangerous activities, wild animals, products).
Manufacturing defect = this unit differs from intended design. Design defect = all units are defective because design is unreasonably dangerous.

Defamation focuses on reputation harm from false statements. False light focuses on mental distress from false impressions. False light requires widespread publication; defamation requires only publication to one third party.
Private nuisance protects individual's use of their property. Public nuisance protects rights common to the public; private party needs special damage to sue.
Fraud requires scienter (knowledge of falsity or recklessness). Negligent misrepresentation requires only failure to use reasonable care. Negligent misrep has narrower scope of liability.

frequentlyTestedAreas: Standard of care (reasonable person, professionals, children)
Products liability (three theories, three defect types)
Defenses to intentional torts (self-defense, necessity, consent)
Defamation and constitutional standards (public figure analysis)
Strict liability for abnormally dangerous activities

subjects.name: Contracts
subjects.overview: Contracts governs the formation, performance, and enforcement of legally binding agreements. Key distinction: Common Law governs services and real property; UCC Article 2 governs sale of goods.

subtopics.name: Mutual Assent - Overview
subtopics.rule: A valid contract requires mutual assent: an offer and acceptance, creating a 'meeting of the minds.'
subtopics.objectiveTheory: Contract formation is judged by outward, objective manifestations of intent, not secret subjective intentions.
subtopics.mnemonics: Contract = Offer + Acceptance + Consideration (OAC)
subtopics.essayTips: Always analyze whether a valid offer was made and properly accepted. Look for ambiguities that could defeat mutual assent. Apply objective theory - what would a reasonable person understand?
subtopics.mbeTips: Objective theory is key - look at what was said/written, not secret intent. Jokes may create contracts if reasonable person would take seriously.

subtopics.name: Offer
subtopics.rule: An offer is a manifestation of willingness to enter into a bargain, creating a power of acceptance in the offeree.
elements: 1. Manifestation of intent - Objective intention to be bound
2. Definiteness - Essential terms are certain or determinable
3. Communication - Offer must be communicated to offeree

ucc: UCC fills gaps for other terms (reasonable price, reasonable time)

notOffers: Advertisements (generally invitations to deal, not offers)
subtopics.mnemonics: Offer = Present intent to be bound NOW (not just negotiating)
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish offers from invitations to deal. Check definiteness - common law stricter than UCC. Advertisements rarely offers unless specific terms + limited quantity. Communication required.
subtopics.mbeTips: UCC requires only quantity term. Ads = usually not offers (exception: specific + limited quantity). Look for language showing intent to be bound NOW.

subtopics.name: Termination of Offer
subtopics.rule: An offer can be terminated before acceptance by various means.

methods.rule: Offeror may revoke any time before acceptance
methods.effective: When received by offeree (or offeree learns from reliable source)
limitations: UCC Firm Offer (merchant's signed writing, up to 3 months)

methods.rule: Offer terminates after stated time or reasonable time if none stated
Death of either party terminates offer (exception: irrevocable offers)
Offer terminates if subject matter destroyed before acceptance
Offer terminates if performance becomes illegal before acceptance

subtopics.mnemonics: Revocation terminates UNLESS: Option, Firm Offer, Reliance, Unilateral performance begun (OFRU)
subtopics.essayTips: Check timing - was acceptance effective before termination? Know the irrevocable offer exceptions. UCC Firm Offer is commonly tested. Detrimental reliance can make offer irrevocable under Restatement.
subtopics.mbeTips: Revocation effective on receipt. Firm Offer = merchant + signed writing + up to 3 months. Option requires consideration. Death terminates non-irrevocable offers automatically.

subtopics.name: Acceptance
subtopics.rule: Acceptance is a manifestation of assent to the terms of an offer in the manner invited or required by the offer.
requirements: 1. By proper offeree (or their authorized agent)
2. Unequivocal acceptance (common law) / Any reasonable manner (UCC)
3. Communicated to offeror (if required)

mannerOfAcceptance.bilateralContract: Acceptance by promise - acceptance effective when dispatched (mailbox rule)
mannerOfAcceptance.unilateralContract: Acceptance by performance only - acceptance upon completion of performance

mailboxRule.rule: Acceptance is effective when dispatched (put in mail), not when received
exceptions: Rejection dispatched before acceptance (first to arrive governs)
Offeree takes benefit of services knowing compensation expected
Offer states silence is acceptance AND offeree intends to accept

subtopics.mnemonics: Mailbox Rule = Acceptance 'drops in the mail,' revocation 'received in hand'
subtopics.essayTips: Apply mailbox rule carefully. Check if acceptance matches offer terms (common law mirror image rule). UCC is more flexible. Unilateral contracts - performance only, not promise.
subtopics.mbeTips: Mailbox rule: acceptance effective on dispatch. Revocation effective on receipt. Silence rarely acceptance. UCC allows acceptance in any reasonable manner.

subtopics.name: Mirror Image Rule vs. UCC Battle of Forms

commonLawRule.rule: Acceptance must mirror offer exactly; any deviation is counteroffer

ucc2207.rule: UCC § 2-207 - Definite expression of acceptance operates as acceptance even with additional/different terms

betweenMerchants.additionalTerms: Become part of contract UNLESS: (1) offer expressly limits acceptance to its terms, (2) terms materially alter, or (3) offeror objects within reasonable time
betweenMerchants.materialAlterations: Arbitration clauses, warranty disclaimers, limitations on remedies

ucc2207.nonMerchants: Additional terms are proposals only; require assent to be included
ucc2207.knockout: If writings don't agree and conduct shows contract, terms on which writings agree + UCC gap-fillers

subtopics.mnemonics: Common Law = Mirror; UCC 2-207 = 'Additional terms sneak in for merchants'
subtopics.essayTips: First identify: Common Law or UCC? If UCC, analyze 2-207 carefully. Check if both parties are merchants. Identify additional vs. different terms. Material alterations don't become part of contract.
subtopics.mbeTips: Know 2-207 cold. Material alterations (arbitration, warranty disclaimer) don't become part of contract. Both merchants needed for additional terms to enter contract.

subtopics.name: Consideration - Elements
subtopics.rule: Consideration is a bargained-for exchange of legal value (benefit to promisor or detriment to promisee).
elements: 1. Bargained-for exchange - Promise induces detriment AND detriment induces promise
2. Legal value - Detriment to promisee OR benefit to promisor
legalDetriment: Doing something not legally obligated to do
Refraining from something legally entitled to do
subtopics.adequacy: Courts do not inquire into adequacy of consideration - peppercorn is sufficient
subtopics.mnemonics: Consideration = 'I give to get' (bargained exchange)
subtopics.essayTips: Look for the exchange - both sides must give something. Past consideration fails. Pre-existing duty issues are common. Gift promises lack consideration.
subtopics.mbeTips: Adequacy doesn't matter - any detriment is enough. Must be bargained for - not a gift or past action. Both parties must give something.

subtopics.name: Consideration Problems

issues.rule: Past actions cannot serve as consideration for a new promise
issues.reason: No bargain - action already occurred, not induced by new promise
exceptions: Promise to pay debt barred by statute of limitations
Promise to pay debt discharged in bankruptcy

issues.rule: Doing or promising what you're already obligated to do is not consideration

modifications.ucc: Modifications in good faith need no new consideration

exceptions: Unforeseen circumstances making performance more difficult
Third party promise to pay for existing duty

issues.rule: Promise that reserves complete discretion to perform or not is illusory - not consideration
examples: 'I'll buy if I feel like it'
Unfettered termination at will without notice
notIllusory: Satisfaction clauses (judged by reasonable person or good faith)
Conditional promises (condition is outside promisor's control)

subtopics.mnemonics: Pre-existing duty = 'Doing what you're already supposed to do doesn't count'
subtopics.essayTips: Watch for modification issues - common law requires consideration, UCC needs only good faith. Requirements contracts are NOT illusory because of good faith. Past consideration = no consideration.
subtopics.mbeTips: UCC modifications need no consideration - key distinction! Requirements contracts are valid. Pre-existing duty exceptions are narrow. Past consideration fails.

subtopics.name: Substitutes for Consideration

substitutes.name: Promissory Estoppel
substitutes.rule: A promise is enforceable without consideration if necessary to prevent injustice when promisor should reasonably expect reliance and promisee does rely to their detriment.
elements: 1. Promise - Clear and definite promise
2. Foreseeable reliance - Promisor should expect reliance
3. Actual reliance - Promisee actually relied
4. Detriment - Reliance caused detriment
5. Injustice - Enforcement necessary to avoid injustice
substitutes.damages: May be limited to reliance damages (not expectation)

substitutes.name: Moral Obligation (Material Benefit)
substitutes.rule: Promise to pay for benefit previously received is enforceable if necessary to prevent injustice
requirements: Promisor received material benefit
Promise made in recognition of benefit
Not a gift; no adequate opportunity to negotiate
substitutes.example: Promise to pay someone who saved your life

substitutes.name: Seal (Historical)
substitutes.rule: At common law, a sealed instrument required no consideration; most jurisdictions have abolished this

subtopics.mnemonics: Promissory Estoppel = 'Promise + Reliance + Injustice'
subtopics.essayTips: Promissory estoppel is a fallback when consideration fails. Damages may be limited. Charitable subscriptions often enforced via promissory estoppel. Moral obligation doctrine is limited.
subtopics.mbeTips: Promissory estoppel requires foreseeable, actual, detrimental reliance. Remedy may be limited to reliance rather than expectation. Charitable promises may be enforced.

subtopics.name: Statute of Frauds
subtopics.rule: Certain contracts must be evidenced by a signed writing to be enforceable.

categoriesMYLEGS.rule: Contracts made in consideration of marriage (not mutual promises to marry)
Contracts that cannot be performed within one year from making
categoriesMYLEGS.note: Measured from CONTRACT formation, not start of performance; if POSSIBLE to complete in one year, SOF doesn't apply

categoriesMYLEGS.rule: Contracts for sale or transfer of interest in land
categoriesMYLEGS.includes: Sales, mortgages, easements, leases over one year

categoriesMYLEGS.rule: Promise by executor to pay estate debts from personal funds

exceptions: Merchant confirmatory memo (both merchants, no objection in 10 days)

categoriesMYLEGS.rule: Promise to answer for debt of another (guarantee)
categoriesMYLEGS.mainPurposeException: If guarantor's main purpose is their own benefit, no writing required

writingRequirement.commonLaw: Signed writing identifying parties, subject matter, essential terms
writingRequirement.ucc: Writing indicating contract, quantity term, signed by party to be charged

subtopics.mnemonics: MY LEGS = Marriage, Year, Land, Executor, Goods $500+, Surety
subtopics.essayTips: First check if SOF applies. Then check if exception applies. One-year rule: if any possibility of performance within one year, SOF doesn't apply. Part performance doctrine for land is frequently tested.
subtopics.mbeTips: One-year rule is measured from CONTRACT date. Look for possibility of completion within one year. Land = possession + payment + improvements. UCC = $500, quantity required.

subtopics.name: Capacity
subtopics.rule: Parties must have legal capacity to enter into a binding contract.

categories.rule: Contracts with minors are voidable at minor's option
categories.disaffirmance: Minor can disaffirm during minority or within reasonable time after reaching majority
categories.ratification: Minor can ratify upon reaching majority (express words or conduct)
categories.necessaries: Minor liable for reasonable value of necessaries (food, shelter, clothing, medical care)
categories.restitution: Upon disaffirmance, minor must return what they still have; split on depreciation

categories.rule: Contract voidable if party unable to understand nature and consequences
tests: Cognitive test: Unable to understand nature and consequences
Volitional test: Unable to act reasonably AND other party has reason to know

categories.rule: Contract voidable if party so intoxicated they don't understand the nature of the transaction AND other party knew or should have known

subtopics.mnemonics: Minors can Make contracts but Might void them (voidable, not void)
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish void from voidable. Minors liable for necessaries at reasonable value. Mental incapacity = cognitive OR volitional test. Intoxication requires other party's knowledge.
subtopics.mbeTips: Minor's contracts are VOIDABLE, not void. Necessaries exception - reasonable value, not contract price. Disaffirmance must return benefits if still possessed.

subtopics.name: Duress and Undue Influence

types.rule: Contract is VOID if induced by physical compulsion
Contract is VOIDABLE if induced by wrongful threat leaving no reasonable alternative
elements: 1. Wrongful or improper threat
2. No reasonable alternative but to agree
3. Threat induced the contract

types.rule: Contract voidable if party in dominant position uses unfair persuasion

subtopics.mnemonics: Physical Duress = Void (gun to head); Economic Duress = Voidable (no choice)
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish physical (void) from economic (voidable). Economic duress requires no reasonable alternative. Undue influence often involves elderly or ill persons. Confidential relationships are key factor.
subtopics.mbeTips: Physical duress = void contract. Economic duress needs wrongful threat + no alternatives. Undue influence looks at relationship + unfair persuasion.

subtopics.name: Misrepresentation and Fraud

types.rule: Contract voidable if induced by knowing or reckless misrepresentation of material fact justifiably relied upon
elements: 1. Misrepresentation of material fact (or fraudulent opinion)
2. Scienter (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard)
3. Intent to induce reliance
4. Justifiable reliance
5. Resulting damages

types.rule: Contract voidable if induced by material misrepresentation, even if innocently made
Generally no duty to disclose; contract may be voidable if:

remedies: Damages (benefit of the bargain or out-of-pocket)
subtopics.mnemonics: Fraud = False statement + Reliance = Rescission
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish fraud (scienter) from innocent misrepresentation. Both can void contract. Analyze whether there was duty to disclose. Material = would affect reasonable person's decision.
subtopics.mbeTips: Fraud requires scienter. Innocent misrepresentation also grounds for rescission. Look for concealment or half-truths. Reliance must be justifiable.

subtopics.name: Mistake

types.rule: Contract voidable if both parties share mistaken belief about basic assumption material to the exchange
elements: 1. Mistake about existing fact (not future conditions)
2. Both parties share same mistake
3. Mistake concerns basic assumption
4. Material effect on exchange
5. Adversely affected party did not bear risk
types.example: Both parties believe painting is copy when it's an original

types.rule: Contract voidable only if non-mistaken party knew or should have known of mistake, OR enforcement would be unconscionable
types.generalRule: Unilateral mistake is NOT grounds for rescission unless other party knew or should have known

riskAllocation.rule: No relief if mistaken party bears risk of mistake
bearingRisk: Agreement allocates risk to that party
Aware of limited knowledge but treated as sufficient

subtopics.mnemonics: Mutual Mistake = Both wrong on BASIC assumption = voidable; Unilateral = Usually stuck
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish mutual from unilateral mistake. Mutual mistake requires shared basic assumption. Unilateral requires other party's knowledge or unconscionability. Check who bears risk of mistake.
subtopics.mbeTips: Mutual mistake = both wrong, contract voidable. Unilateral = generally no relief unless other party knew. Basic assumption = material foundation of deal.

subtopics.name: Unconscionability
subtopics.rule: Contract or clause may be unenforceable if unconscionable at time of formation.

types.rule: Unfairness in bargaining process
Unfairness in the terms themselves

subtopics.requirement: Most courts require BOTH procedural and substantive elements (sliding scale)
subtopics.mnemonics: Unconscionability = Unfair PROCESS + Unfair TERMS
subtopics.essayTips: Analyze BOTH procedural and substantive elements. Courts use sliding scale - more of one can compensate for less of other. Determined at time of formation, not later. Judge decides, not jury.
subtopics.mbeTips: Need both procedural AND substantive (sliding scale). Determined at CONTRACT formation. Unequal bargaining power alone is insufficient. Judge, not jury, decides.

subtopics.name: Illegality and Public Policy

rules.rule: Contracts to commit illegal acts are void and unenforceable
examples: Contract to commit crime
Gambling contracts (where illegal)
Contracts in restraint of trade

rules.rule: Contracts violating public policy may be unenforceable
factors: Likelihood that refusing enforcement furthers policy

effects.generalRule: Court leaves parties where it finds them - no recovery
exceptions: Party not equally at fault (in pari delicto)

covenantNotToCompete.employment: Enforceable if reasonable in scope (geography, time, activities)
covenantNotToCompete.saleBusiness: Generally more freely enforced as part of goodwill sale
covenantNotToCompete.modification: Many courts will 'blue pencil' to make reasonable

subtopics.mnemonics: Illegal = Void, court won't help either party
subtopics.essayTips: Identify the illegality or policy violation. Check if severance is possible. Non-compete reasonableness is frequently tested. Some states (CA) ban non-competes.
subtopics.mbeTips: Illegal contracts = void and unenforceable. Court won't assist either party. Non-competes must be reasonable. Some states allow blue penciling.

subtopics.name: Parol Evidence Rule
subtopics.rule: A final written agreement may not be contradicted or supplemented by prior or contemporaneous agreements.

integration.test: Writing is intended as final and complete statement of terms
integration.effect: Bars all prior/contemporaneous agreements on same subject

integration.test: Writing is final but not complete
integration.effect: Cannot contradict but may supplement with consistent additional terms

exceptionsAlwaysAdmissible: Course of dealing, usage of trade, course of performance (UCC)
subtopics.uccApproach: More liberal - admits course of dealing, usage of trade, course of performance to explain or supplement
subtopics.mnemonics: Parol Evidence = Prior promises are Pushed out by Paper
subtopics.essayTips: First determine if writing is complete or partial integration. Complete = can't add or contradict. Partial = can add consistent terms. ALWAYS analyze exceptions. UCC is more permissive.
subtopics.mbeTips: Complete integration bars contradiction AND supplementation. Partial bars contradiction only. Formation defects always admissible. UCC admits trade usage, course of dealing.

subtopics.name: Interpretation Principles
rules: Handwritten terms control typed; typed control printed
All provisions should be given effect if possible
Course of performance > course of dealing > usage of trade (UCC)
subtopics.extrinsicEvidence: Admissible to interpret ambiguous terms, even in integrated agreements
subtopics.essayTips: Look for ambiguities to allow in extrinsic evidence. Apply canons of construction. Note who drafted the agreement.
subtopics.mbeTips: Plain meaning first. Ambiguity construed against drafter. Specific beats general. UCC hierarchy: performance > dealing > trade usage.

subtopics.name: Third Party Beneficiaries
subtopics.rule: A third party may enforce a contract made for their benefit if they are an intended beneficiary.

types.test: Promisor's performance intended to benefit third party (not just incidentally)

subtypes.name: Creditor Beneficiary
subtypes.definition: Performance will satisfy promisee's debt to beneficiary

subtypes.name: Donee Beneficiary
subtypes.definition: Performance intended as gift to beneficiary

types.rights: Can enforce contract once rights have vested

types.definition: Benefits from performance but wasn't intended purpose

vesting.rule: Parties can modify/rescind until beneficiary's rights vest
vestingOccurs: Beneficiary learns of contract and assents
Beneficiary materially changes position in reliance

subtopics.defenses: Promisor may assert against beneficiary any defense promisor could have against promisee
subtopics.mnemonics: Intended = 'I' can sue; Incidental = 'I' cannot
subtopics.essayTips: First classify as intended or incidental. Check if rights vested - if not, contract can be modified. Analyze promisor's defenses. Creditor vs. donee distinction matters for vesting.
subtopics.mbeTips: Incidental beneficiaries have NO rights. Rights vest upon reliance, assent, or lawsuit. Promisor can raise any defense against promisee.

subtopics.name: Assignment of Rights
subtopics.rule: Assignment is the transfer of rights under a contract to a third party (assignee).
subtopics.generalRule: All contract rights are assignable unless:
exceptions: Assignment materially impairs obligor's chance of return performance

antiAssignmentClauses.generalRule: Clause prohibiting assignment is construed to bar only delegation, not assignment of right to payment
antiAssignmentClauses.effect: Assignment in breach of clause is valid but may be breach of contract

assignee: Subject to all defenses obligor could raise against assignor
Not subject to defenses arising AFTER assignment if obligor has notice
obligor: Must perform for assignee after notice
Payment to assignor before notice is valid

multipleAssignees.commonLaw: First in time, first in right
multipleAssignees.modernRule: First to give notice prevails if took for value without notice of prior assignment

subtopics.mnemonics: Assignment = 'A' gives rights to 'B'; Delegation = 'A' gives duties to 'B'
subtopics.essayTips: Check if assignment is prohibited. Assignee takes subject to defenses. Obligor needs notice before required to perform to assignee. Anti-assignment clauses narrowly construed.
