subtopics.mbeTips: Assignee stands in assignor's shoes - takes subject to defenses. Notice to obligor is important. Anti-assignment clauses don't bar right to payment usually.

subtopics.name: Delegation of Duties
subtopics.rule: Delegation is the transfer of performance duties under a contract to a third party (delegate).
subtopics.generalRule: All contract duties are delegable unless:
exceptions: Other party has substantial interest in having original party perform (personal services)

effects.delegator: Remains liable unless other party agrees to novation
effects.delegate: Liable to obligee only if delegate assumes duty for consideration (promisee can enforce as third party beneficiary)

novation.rule: Agreement releasing delegator and substituting delegate as new party
novation.requirements: Obligee must agree to release delegator

subtopics.mnemonics: Delegation = 'D' delegates Duties; Delegator still liable (no free pass)
subtopics.essayTips: Delegator remains liable unless novation. Personal services cannot be delegated. Assumption creates liability to obligee. Distinguish from assignment (rights vs. duties).
subtopics.mbeTips: Delegator stays liable unless novation. Personal services are non-delegable. Assumption by delegate creates third party beneficiary rights.

subtopics.name: Types of Conditions
subtopics.rule: A condition is an event, not certain to occur, that must occur before performance becomes due.

types.rule: Must occur BEFORE performance is due
types.example: 'I'll buy the house if it passes inspection'

types.rule: Terminates duty to perform AFTER it has become absolute
types.example: 'Insurance coverage terminated if not notified within 30 days of loss'

types.rule: Each party's performance is conditioned on other's simultaneous performance
types.example: Sale of goods - delivery and payment concurrent

sources.rule: Explicitly stated in contract; must be strictly complied with
Implied by law to do justice; substantial performance may suffice

satisfactionClauses.objectiveStandard: Mechanical/commercial contracts - judged by reasonable person
satisfactionClauses.subjectiveStandard: Aesthetic/personal contracts - genuine satisfaction required (good faith)

subtopics.mnemonics: Express condition = exact compliance; Implied condition = substantial OK
subtopics.essayTips: Identify condition type (precedent, subsequent, concurrent). Express conditions require strict compliance. Constructive conditions need only substantial performance. Satisfaction clauses - determine objective vs. subjective standard.
subtopics.mbeTips: Express = strict compliance. Implied = substantial performance may suffice. Condition precedent shifts burden to prove occurrence. Look for condition language ('if,' 'provided that').

subtopics.name: Excuse of Conditions

methods.retraction: Can be retracted unless other party relied

methods.rule: Condition excused if party whose performance is conditioned wrongfully prevents occurrence
If obligor repudiates, obligee's conditions excused
Statement that condition won't be insisted upon, followed by detrimental reliance
Court may excuse condition if enforcement would cause disproportionate forfeiture

subtopics.mnemonics: Excuses = WPAEF (Waiver, Prevention, Anticipatory repudiation, Estoppel, Forfeiture)
subtopics.essayTips: Look for conduct suggesting waiver. Prevention/hindrance is common issue. Forfeiture requires disproportionate harm. Waiver can be retracted if no reliance.
subtopics.mbeTips: Waiver = voluntary relinquishment. Prevention/hindrance excuses the condition. Forfeiture doctrine prevents unjust results. Retraction of waiver allowed if no reliance.

subtopics.name: Substantial Performance
subtopics.rule: A party who substantially performs is entitled to contract price minus damages for deviation.
requirements: Performance must be close to complete
Defects must be minor and unintentional
Essential purpose of contract must be fulfilled
subtopics.recovery: Contract price minus cost of completion or diminution in value
subtopics.uccPerfectTender: For goods, perfect tender rule applies - buyer can reject for any defect (with exceptions)
subtopics.mnemonics: Substantial = 'Close enough' for common law; UCC = Perfect tender
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish common law (substantial performance) from UCC (perfect tender). Check if breach was willful. Calculate damages: contract price minus cost to complete.
subtopics.mbeTips: Substantial performance applies to services/construction (common law). UCC uses perfect tender. Willful breach = no substantial performance.

subtopics.name: Material Breach
subtopics.rule: A material breach is a failure of performance that substantially defeats the purpose of the contract.
factors: Extent to which injured party is deprived of expected benefit
Extent to which injured party can be compensated
Good or bad faith of breaching party
effects: If breach is total, non-breaching party is discharged and may sue immediately
Non-breaching party still entitled to sue for damages
subtopics.partialBreach: Non-breaching party must continue performance but may sue for damages from partial breach
subtopics.mnemonics: Material Breach = Major failure = Other party can walk away
subtopics.essayTips: Apply factors to determine materiality. Material breach excuses other party's performance. Partial breach doesn't excuse - only damages. Time is of the essence = material if missed.
subtopics.mbeTips: Material breach = other party can suspend/cancel. Partial breach = must continue, can sue. 'Time is of the essence' makes delays material.

subtopics.name: Anticipatory Repudiation
subtopics.rule: An unequivocal statement or conduct indicating party will not perform when due.
requirements: Statement must be clear and unequivocal
Must relate to material obligation
Must be before performance is due
responses: Treat as immediate breach and sue
Ignore and wait for performance date

conditions: Other party has not materially changed position
Other party has not indicated repudiation is accepted

uccAdequateAssurance.rule: If reasonable grounds for insecurity, party may demand adequate assurance and suspend performance
uccAdequateAssurance.failure: Failure to provide assurance within 30 days is repudiation (UCC)

subtopics.mnemonics: Anticipatory Repudiation = 'Advance notice I won't perform' = Immediate breach
subtopics.essayTips: Statement must be CLEAR and UNEQUIVOCAL. Mere expressions of doubt insufficient. Check if retraction possible. UCC allows demanding assurance if insecure.
subtopics.mbeTips: Must be clear and unequivocal - doubt isn't enough. Retraction allowed until other party relies or accepts. UCC: demand assurance, 30 days to respond.

subtopics.name: UCC Perfect Tender Rule
subtopics.rule: For sale of goods, if goods or tender fail in any respect to conform to contract, buyer may reject whole, accept whole, or accept any commercial unit and reject rest.

exceptions.rule: Seller may cure defective tender if time for performance hasn't expired or seller reasonably believed goods would be acceptable
Buyer can reject only if defect substantially impairs that installment and cannot be cured; can cancel only if defect substantially impairs whole contract
Buyer who accepted can later revoke if defect substantially impairs value and was latent or buyer reasonably relied on seller's assurance of cure

occurs: Failure to reject within reasonable time
Doing any act inconsistent with seller's ownership
acceptanceOfGoods.effect: Buyer must pay contract price but can recover damages for non-conformity

subtopics.mnemonics: Perfect Tender = Any defect = right to reject (but seller may cure)
subtopics.essayTips: Perfect tender for single delivery; substantial performance for installments. Seller's right to cure is important. Acceptance limits buyer to damages. Revocation requires substantial impairment + justification.
subtopics.mbeTips: Single delivery = perfect tender. Installments = substantial impairment. Cure allowed if time remains or seller reasonably expected acceptance. Revocation = substantial impairment required.

subtopics.name: Impossibility
subtopics.rule: Performance is excused when it becomes objectively impossible due to circumstances beyond party's control.
requirements: Event made performance objectively impossible (not just difficult)
Event was not foreseeable at time of contracting
Risk was not assumed by party seeking excuse

categories.rule: Death/incapacity of person necessary for performance excuses obligation
Destruction of specific subject matter through no fault excuses performance
Performance becoming illegal after formation excuses obligation

subtopics.temporaryImpossibility: Suspends duty; performance required when possibility resumes unless burden materially increased
subtopics.mnemonics: Impossibility = 'Can't be done by anyone' (objective, not subjective)
subtopics.essayTips: Distinguish objective ('no one can do it') from subjective ('I can't do it'). Subjective impossibility no excuse. Must be unforeseeable and unassumed. Temporary impossibility only suspends.
subtopics.mbeTips: Must be OBJECTIVE impossibility. Subjective difficulty is not excuse. Foreseeable events don't excuse. Death excuses personal services only.

subtopics.name: Impracticability
subtopics.rule: Performance excused when supervening event makes performance extremely difficult or costly beyond what was reasonably foreseeable.
elements: 1. Extreme difficulty or expense (not just more burdensome)
2. Due to unforeseen supervening event
3. Non-occurrence of event was basic assumption of contract
4. Party seeking excuse did not assume risk
subtopics.uccApproach: Section 2-615: Failure of presupposed conditions excuses delay or non-delivery
subtopics.mnemonics: Impracticability = 'Extreme hardship' (not just harder/more expensive)
subtopics.essayTips: Higher bar than just 'more difficult.' Analyze whether risk was allocated by contract. Market fluctuations usually not enough. Compare with impossibility - both are excuse doctrines.
subtopics.mbeTips: Extreme burden required - ordinary cost increases not enough. Risk allocation in contract controls. UCC 2-615 applies to goods. Foreseeable = no excuse.

subtopics.name: Frustration of Purpose
subtopics.rule: Performance excused when supervening event substantially frustrates the principal purpose of the contract.
elements: 1. Principal purpose is substantially frustrated
2. By supervening event not reasonably foreseeable
3. Non-occurrence was basic assumption of contract
4. Frustration is substantial (not just less valuable)
subtopics.distinction: Unlike impossibility - performance IS possible but has become pointless
subtopics.example: Coronation cases: Room rented to view parade, parade cancelled - performance possible but purpose frustrated
subtopics.mnemonics: Frustration = 'I CAN do it but now there's no point'
subtopics.essayTips: Key: purpose must be SUBSTANTIALLY frustrated. Purpose must be known to both parties. Performance is still possible - distinguishes from impossibility. Classic coronation cases.
subtopics.mbeTips: Purpose must be principal, known to both, and substantially frustrated. Performance is possible but meaningless. Both parties must know the purpose.

subtopics.name: Modification and Accord

modification.ucc: Modification in good faith needs no consideration (§ 2-209)
modification.statuteOfFrauds: Modification must comply if modified contract falls within SOF

accord.definition: Agreement to accept a different performance than originally owed
accord.satisfaction: Performance of the accord (satisfaction) discharges original duty
accord.effect: Original duty suspended when accord made; discharged when satisfied

novation.definition: Substitution of new party for original party

subtopics.mnemonics: Accord = Agreement for substituted performance; Novation = New party substituted
subtopics.essayTips: UCC vs common law on modification consideration. Accord suspends until satisfaction. Novation requires all parties' consent. Check SOF for modifications.
subtopics.mbeTips: UCC modifications need no consideration - must be good faith. Common law needs consideration. Novation = complete discharge of original party.

subtopics.name: Expectation Damages
subtopics.rule: Damages to put plaintiff in position they would have been in had the contract been performed.
subtopics.formula: Loss in value (what you would have received) + Other loss (consequential/incidental) - Cost avoided - Loss avoided

limitations.rule: Damages must be foreseeable at time of contracting as probable result of breach
types: General damages - arise naturally from breach
Consequential damages - from special circumstances known to breaching party

limitations.rule: Damages must be proven with reasonable certainty
limitations.newBusiness: New business lost profits may be speculative but not barred as matter of law

limitations.rule: Non-breaching party must take reasonable steps to mitigate damages
limitations.cannotRecover: Damages that could have been reasonably avoided

subtopics.mnemonics: Expectation = What you Expected to gain; limited by FCC (Foreseeability, Certainty, mitigation Costs)
subtopics.essayTips: Calculate expectation damages with formula. Apply Hadley v. Baxendale foreseeability test. Check mitigation efforts. New business profits aren't automatically barred.
subtopics.mbeTips: Expectation = benefit of the bargain. Consequential damages must be foreseeable. Mitigation required. Certainty needed for amount.

subtopics.name: Reliance Damages
subtopics.rule: Damages to restore plaintiff to position before the contract, recovering expenditures made in reliance.
subtopics.limitation: Cannot recover reliance damages that would exceed expectation damages (can't turn losing contract into winning)
subtopics.mnemonics: Reliance = What you Relied on and spent
subtopics.essayTips: Alternative to expectation damages. Good choice when lost profits are speculative. Cannot turn bad deal into good deal - capped at expectation. Common in promissory estoppel.
subtopics.mbeTips: Cannot exceed expectation damages. Useful when profits are speculative. Common in promissory estoppel. Pre-contract expenses may be included if in reliance.

subtopics.name: Restitution
subtopics.rule: Damages to restore to plaintiff benefits conferred on defendant, preventing unjust enrichment.
availability: Breaching party in some cases (minus damages caused to other party)
Non-breaching party as alternative to expectation
subtopics.measure: Value of benefit conferred on defendant (not plaintiff's cost)

breachingParty.majorityRule: Breaching party can recover restitution minus damages (to prevent windfall)

subtopics.mnemonics: Restitution = Return what was Received
subtopics.essayTips: Focus on benefit to defendant. Available even without contract. Breaching party recovery is controversial - know both rules. Alternative remedy when contract is unenforceable.
subtopics.mbeTips: Measure is benefit to defendant. Available even to breaching party (modern rule, minus damages). Not limited by contract price.

subtopics.name: Specific Performance
subtopics.rule: Equitable remedy compelling party to perform contract as promised.
requirements: Valid, enforceable contract
Inadequate legal remedy (money damages insufficient)
Feasibility of enforcement
Mutuality of remedy (modern: not absolute requirement)
No equitable defenses (unclean hands, laches)
subtopics.realProperty: Specific performance routinely granted - land is unique
subtopics.goods: Available under UCC for unique goods or other proper circumstances
subtopics.personalServices: Not available for personal services (involuntary servitude, enforcement problems)
subtopics.mnemonics: Specific Performance = 'Do exactly what you promised' (when money won't work)
subtopics.essayTips: Land = presumptively unique. Personal services = never specific performance. UCC: unique goods or proper circumstances. Check for equitable defenses. Analyze adequacy of legal remedy.
subtopics.mbeTips: Real property = specific performance. Personal services = no. Unique goods = yes. Check feasibility and equitable defenses.

subtopics.name: Liquidated Damages
subtopics.rule: Pre-agreed damages provision enforceable if reasonable estimate of harm and actual damages difficult to ascertain.
requirements: 1. Damages were difficult to estimate at time of contracting
2. Amount is reasonable forecast of harm
3. Not a penalty
subtopics.penalty: If amount is disproportionate to actual/anticipated harm, it's an unenforceable penalty

reasonablenessTest.secondRestatement: Reasonable at time of contracting OR in light of actual loss

subtopics.mnemonics: Liquidated Damages = 'Let's agree now' (if reasonable, not penalty)
subtopics.essayTips: Apply two-part test: difficulty of estimation + reasonableness. Compare to actual damages if known. Courts dislike penalties. UCC similar approach but may consider actual harm.
subtopics.mbeTips: Must be reasonable estimate when contract formed. Penalty clauses unenforceable. Actual harm may be considered in some jurisdictions.

subtopics.name: UCC Buyer's Remedies

remedies.rule: Buy substitute goods and recover difference from contract price (§ 2-712)
remedies.formula: Cover price - Contract price + Incidental/Consequential damages

remedies.rule: If no cover, recover market-contract differential (§ 2-713)
remedies.formula: Market price (at time of breach) - Contract price + Incidental/Consequential damages

remedies.rule: Available for unique goods or other proper circumstances
Recovery of identified goods when cover unavailable

subtopics.incidentalDamages: Expenses incident to breach (inspection, receipt, custody of rejected goods)
subtopics.consequentialDamages: Foreseeable losses from breach (lost profits, other damages)
subtopics.mnemonics: Buyer's Remedies: CMSRC (Cover, Market, Specific performance, Replevin, Consequential)
subtopics.essayTips: Cover is preferred remedy. Market damages use market price at breach. Consequential damages must be foreseeable. Specific performance for unique goods.
subtopics.mbeTips: Cover must be in good faith and reasonable. Market damages when no cover. Both incidental AND consequential available to buyers.

remedies.rule: Resell goods and recover difference from contract price (§ 2-706)
remedies.formula: Contract price - Resale price + Incidental damages
